content: The abstract discusses the findings of a clinical trial on the use of Truvada, a medication commonly used to treat HIV infections, as a daily pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) to prevent HIV transmission. The trial demonstrated that Truvada was 42% effective in preventing HIV infections among sexually active men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender individuals. The AIDS Healthcare Foundation (AHF) conducted a study to evaluate the acceptability of PrEP among these populations. To assess acceptability, AHF developed an online questionnaire, which was administered by a third-party marketing research firm. Participants were screened for eligibility, requiring them to be over 18 years old and identify as gay, bisexual, MSM, or transgender. Participation was voluntary. The survey was completed by 822 male and transgender respondents from racially diverse backgrounds: 32% White, 30% Hispanic/Latino, 15% Black/African American, and 23% Asian/Pacific Islander or Native American. The majority of respondents (51%) were aged between 30 and 54 years. Among the 665 respondents (81%) who reported being sexually active, 24% stated they never or rarely used condoms. Overall, 79% of participants expressed willingness to take a daily pill that was more than 90% effective at preventing HIV infections. However, acceptability dropped to 69% when participants were asked about taking the pill daily in conjunction with monthly HIV/STD testing. When asked about paying a $60 co-pay to cover the cost of the medication and laboratory tests, only 41% indicated they would be willing to take the pill. The study concluded that under real-life conditions, including co-pays, doctor visits, and laboratory testing, the acceptability of PrEP decreased significantly. Further research is needed to understand the acceptability of PrEP, especially given that clinical trials have shown only partial efficacy in preventing HIV infections. Another study assessed knowledge and attitudes toward PrEP among a sample of sexually active MSM in New York City following the publication of the iPrEx study, which demonstrated partial efficacy of PrEP. A street-intercept survey conducted during New York City's 2011 Gay Pride events included 480 men who reported having sex with other men in the preceding six months. Only 8% of participants had heard of PrEP, with Black and HIV-positive men being the most likely to have knowledge of it. Many participants expressed concerns that the availability of PrEP might lead to decreased condom use among gay men. Men who believed PrEP had significant side effects were the least likely to express interest in using it. The study highlighted the need for informational campaigns targeting potential PrEP users. A global online survey conducted in 2010 among 5,046 MSM assessed knowledge and interest in PrEP and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). The survey revealed that 53% and 60% of MSM reported no knowledge of PEP and PrEP, respectively. However, 70% and 74% expressed strong interest in using PEP and PrEP to prevent HIV. Predictors of PrEP awareness included older age, having had a physical examination, prior HIV testing, recent condom use, and higher perceived PrEP effectiveness. Interest in participating in a PrEP trial was associated with younger age, living in Latin America, and willingness to use an HIV home test. The study concluded that while knowledge of PrEP was limited, there was substantial interest in its use, emphasizing the need for efforts to disseminate information about PrEP. A study conducted among MSM in Germany found that over 50% of participants were aware of PrEP, and more than 75% expressed willingness to use it. However, only 5% had used PrEP previously. The findings underscored the urgent need for more information on PrEP to address gaps in knowledge and promote its use. In Kenya, a survey of community opinions and preferences regarding new prevention technologies (NPTs), including PrEP, microbicides, and vaccines, revealed mixed reactions. The majority of respondents preferred injectable PrEP (67%) and indicated that product characteristics, cost, accessibility, side effects, efficacy, and associated stigma influenced their preferences. The study emphasized the importance of understanding evolving community preferences to guide the introduction and implementation of NPTs. A qualitative study in the United States explored healthcare providers' perspectives on implementing PrEP in clinical settings. Providers reported little or no demand for PrEP from patients at the time of the study. They expressed differing opinions on the most appropriate candidates for PrEP and highlighted challenges related to cost, office capacity, dosing schedules, and patient follow-up. The study recommended developing clinical protocols to support and monitor adherence to PrEP among patients.
